title: Object Pool pattern
idea: The Object Pool pattern keeps a fixed set of costly, reusable objects; callers borrow one, use it, and return it instead of creating their own.
points: Pool objects that are slow to create and limited: connections, threads, sockets.
The pool size caps concurrency; when all are busy, callers wait with a timeout.
`release` must reset state, or the next borrower inherits the last one's settings.
The JDK pools threads in `ThreadPoolExecutor`; HikariCP pools JDBC connections.

steps.caption: The pool creates two connections up front. No request pays the setup cost later.
Thread A calls `acquire` and borrows connection 1 from the queue head.
Thread B borrows connection 2. The idle queue is now empty.
Thread C calls `acquire` and blocks. The pool size caps load on the database.
Thread A calls `release`. The pool resets the connection, then puts it back.
Thread C wakes and takes the same connection object, clean.
Thread D waits, but nothing returns before its timeout.
The timeout expires and `acquire` throws. D fails fast instead of hanging forever.

code.title: The problem: open per request
code.caption: Every request opens its own connection: the setup cost repeats and nothing limits the total.

walk.text: The database accepts a fixed number of open connections. Each `open` stands in for a slow handshake.
Sequential requests never overload it, but each one repeats the full setup cost.
The loop holds 25 connections open at once, as a burst of requests would. Nothing caps it.
The database refuses the extra request. The app learns its limit only from a failure.

code.title: The fix: a bounded pool
code.caption: A thread-safe pool on an `ArrayBlockingQueue`: eager creation, timed acquire, reset on release.

walk.text: The constructor validates the size and creates every connection once. The queue is thread-safe.
`poll` with a timeout blocks until a connection returns, then gives up with a clear error.
`release` resets state first. A full queue catches some double releases, not all; real pools track borrowed objects.
`try`/`finally` returns the connection even when the work throws. Leaks drain a pool silently.
Eight tasks on four threads share two connections. Printing counts and a bound keeps output stable.
With both connections held, a third `acquire` times out after 50 ms.
The tenant schema set by the last user is gone after release.

pitfalls: Skipping `release` on an exception path leaks objects until every caller times out.
Returning objects without a reset leaks the previous user's schema, session or buffer contents.
Pooling cheap objects like DTOs or `StringBuilder` adds locking and stale state for no gain.

quiz.q: Same `ConnectionPool` as the demo. What does this print?
quiz.why: A pool of one lends the same object again, so `c == d`. `release` reset the schema. The caller still holding `c` is a bug waiting to happen.

takeaway: Pool only costly, limited objects; always release in `finally`, and reset on return.
